title: Just 10 Minutes of Forest Birdsong May Relieve Stress
paragraphs: Feeling stressed? A new study from the United States suggests that just 10 minutes of listening to birdsong in a forest may help.

The study was carried out by researchers at North Carolina State University, led by Professor Nils Peterson, and it was published in the journal Environmental Conservation in 2026. It involved 106 students at the university.

The researchers wanted to find out how much the setting and the sounds around people affect their stress levels. The students sat in two different outdoor places. One was a forest on the university campus, which had been restored in 2006 from a damaged area along a creek. The other was a paved plaza next to a road intersection. In each place, the students wore noise-canceling headphones and listened to 10 minutes of birdsong and 10 minutes of traffic noise. Afterward, they rated their stress levels, their emotions and how mentally refreshed they felt.

The results were clear. When students were in the forest listening to birdsong, their average stress score was 3.2 on an 11-point scale. In contrast, when they were in the plaza listening to traffic, their average score was 6.4, twice as high. The forest with birdsong also produced the most positive emotions and the strongest feeling of being refreshed.

Interestingly, both the setting and the sound mattered on their own. For example, listening to birdsong in the plaza or traffic noise in the forest produced results somewhere in the middle. For stress and emotions, the place and the sound were roughly equally important.

According to Peterson, there were significant effects for participants who were in a green space listening to birds. Cindy Frantz, a psychologist at Oberlin College who was not involved in the study, said that the effects were large and likely to make a real difference.

However, Frantz also pointed out that a single study cannot show how long the effects last, whether people get used to them or whether everyone benefits equally. In addition, other research suggests that some bird sounds, such as loud or harsh calls, may not have the same calming effect.
